new_statements.quote: The Phonological Word in Nyeu may have from one to three syllables. It has one and only one stressed syllable as nucleus, and may have one preceding unstressed or lightly stressed syllable as periphery. [p.29] ... 3.3 Word Stress. Stress in Nyeu is predictable as follows: ... In a monosyllabic word stress is on that one syllable. ... In disyllabic word of Type A ..., of which the first syllable is a presyllable, stress is on the last syllable. ... Type B ..., there is stress on both syllables: primary stress on the last syllable, and secondary stress on the first syllable. [pp.33-34] ... So, in trisyllabic words the primary stress is always on the last syllable of a word. Since stress is predictable it needs not be marked in phonemic writing. [p.36]
new_statements.citation: Taweeporn Suwannaraj. [1980] (Glottolog: 1990). The phonology of the Nyeu language. MA thesis, Faculty of Graduate Studies, Mahidol University.
new_statements.locator: Ch. III sec. 3.1 p. 29 and sec. 3.3 'Word Stress', pp. 33-36 (PDF pp. 43, 47-50); scanned of these pages in
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened the copy we hold (146-pp image-only scan from http://sealang.net/archives/mahidol/Taweeporn.pdf; title page: 'The Phonology of the Nyeu Language' by Taweeporn Suwannaraj, MA thesis, Faculty of Graduate Studies of Mahidol University, date overtyped 1980/1990, ILCRD library stamp) and rendered PDF pp. 1, 15, 43, 47, 48, 50 as page images, plus read the reader's scanned file for pp. 44-46, 49. Every quoted sentence is on the page at the stated locator, verbatim: p. 29 (PDF 43) sec. 3.1 'The Phonological Word in Nyeu may have from one to three syllables. It has one and only one stressed syllable as nucleus, and may have one preceding unstressed or lightly stressed syllable as periphery.'…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and falls on the final (major) syllable of the phonological word (1-3 syllables): presyllables Cə are unstressed; a closed or long-vowel first syllable (and the middle minor syllable of CəCVC.CVC trisyllables) carries secondary stress; primary stress is on the last syllable in mono-, di- and trisyllabic words.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Explicitly described: in disyllabic Types B and C the first (closed or long-vowel / free) syllable has secondary stress; in trisyllabic Type A (Cə.CV(C).CV(C)) secondary stress on the second syllable, in Type B (CV(C).Cə.CV(C)) on the first syllable; presyllables with [ə] are unstressed.
new_statements.exceptions: Disyllabic Type C words (two free syllables) whose first syllable ends in /ʔ/ or /h/ have primary stress on the FIRST syllable and secondary stress on the last, e.g. ['diəʔˌmat] 'tears', ['muhˌmat] 'face' (p. 34); all other Type C words follow the final-stress pattern. Word pitch (high/mid/low) is separately described as predictable from syllable structure (sec. 3.4), i.e. the language is treated as non-tonal.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (max. three syllables: presyllable/minor + major); examples are citation forms; the Word is defined as functioning within the Intonation Group, whose contours are treated separately in ch. II. Variety: Nyeu of Ban Phon Kho, Amphoe Muang, Sisaket. Corroborated second-hand by Thitiporn Phimjun 2004 (Mahidol MA, Thai), pp. 36-38: stress on the second (major) syllable of disyllables in Kuy, Kuay and Nyeu alike, with the unstressed first-syllable vowel reduced to /ə/ in Nyeu.
new_statements.identity_note: Taweeporn's thesis describes Nyeu as spoken at Ban Phon Kho, Amphoe Muang Sisaket, Sisaket Province (main informant Mrs. Samnieng Khamla); this is the language Glottolog codes nyeu1238 / ISO nyl (alt. names Yoe, Yeu; Thai เญอ/เยอ), a West Katuic variety closely related to Kuy/Kuay (kuyy1240). Thitiporn 2004 compares Nyeu with Kuy (Ban Ku) and Kuay (Ban Hai Noi), Prang Ku district, Sisaket. Note the thesis date: Glottolog lists 1990 and a duplicate 1998 record, but the acknowledgements are dated November 1980 and Thitiporn cites it as 1980; the earlier scan's 'archives.sealang.net/mahidol' link is dead but the archive lives at http://sealang.net/archives/mahidol/.

new_statements.quote: 3.3 Word Stress. Stress in Nyeu is predictable as follows: 3.3.1 In Monosyllabic Words. In a monosyllabic word stress is on that one syllable. [...] 3.3.2.1 In disyllabic word of Type A (See sec.3.2.2.1), of which the first syllable is a presyllable, stress is on the last syllable. [p. 33] 3.3.2.2 In disyllabic word of Type B (see sec.3.2.2.2), there is stress on both syllables: primary stress on the last syllable, and secondary stress on the first syllable. [...] 3.3.2.3 In disyllabic words of Type C, (see sec.3.2.2.3), there is stress on both syllables. If the final consonant of the first syllable is ʔ or h, the primary stress is on the first syllable and secondary stress is on the last syllable. [...] All other disyllabic words of Type C have the same stress pattern as Type B [p. 34] So, in trisyllabic words the primary stress is always on the last syllable of a word. Since stress is predictable it needs not be marked in phonemic writing. [p. 36]

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog rule 01 / 001 (final primary stress in di- and trisyllables) and as the existing statement from the same thesis; adds the secondary-stress positions per word type, the ʔ/h-final-first-syllable exception in Type C disyllables (initial primary stress), and the explicit statement that stress is predictable and unmarked. The catalog's 001 for trisyllables is exactly the thesis's 'always on the last syllable' (p. 36).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is on the last syllable of the word: the only syllable of a monosyllable, the major syllable of presyllable+major disyllables (Type A), the final syllable of Type B and Type C disyllables, and the final syllable of all trisyllables. One stated exception: in Type C disyllables (two phonetically free syllables) whose first syllable ends in ʔ or h, primary stress is on the first syllable and secondary on the last (e.g. ['liəʔ ˌluəj] 'chicken coop', ['cuəh ˌmɔːm] 'monk', ['diəʔ ˌmat] 'tears'). Stress is predictable from word structure and is not marked phonemically. Sec. 3.4 adds that word pitch (high/mid/low) is likewise predictable from word structure, i.e. the language is not tonal.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the first syllable of Type B disyllables (closed or long-vowel first syllable, e.g. [ˌpiŋ'waːj] 'spider') and of ordinary Type C disyllables ([ˌɲit'suːt] 'silk cloth'); in trisyllables of Type A (presyllable + minor + major) secondary stress is on the second syllable ([tə ˌlaw'paw] 'to dream'), in Type B (CV(C).Cə.CV(C)) on the first syllable ([ˌkamsə'naː] 'a bow'). Presyllables (Cə) are unstressed and their vowel reduces or drops in fast speech (p. 30).
new_statements.exceptions: Type C disyllables whose first syllable ends in ʔ or h take primary stress on the first syllable and secondary on the last (p. 34, five examples); all other patterns are final-stressed.
new_statements.identity_note: The thesis describes the Nyeu of Ban Phon Kho, Amphoe Muang, Sisaket Province, Thailand (per the note from the first download); Nyeu is a Katuic (West Katuic, Kuy-related) language. No other variety is described.
